# Results — Study 661 (USO-Roll-Decay)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test — **"USO
tracks oil"**: USO holds (mostly front-month) WTI futures, not crude itself, so when the curve
sits in contango each monthly roll sells the cheaper expiring contract and buys the pricier
next-month one — a structural drag that should make the ETF a mechanical loser against the
"oil price" everyone quotes (CL=F, the continuously-rolled NYMEX front-month print) even when
oil itself goes nowhere. Offline & deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py`
to reproduce every number. As-of **2026-06-30** (the last complete calendar month; the partial
current month is dropped). Fingerprints `b9dde5e9cdd0` (USO) / `0e2eae3d2942` (CL=F).*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily USO adjusted close (5,087 rows) + CL=F front-month close (5,087 rows), 2006-04-10 → 2026-06-30 |
| Contango-stress windows | **hardcoded** table of 2 widely-documented episodes: 2008-12-01→2009-06-30 (storage-glut super-contango) and 2020-03-01→2020-06-30 (COVID demand-collapse super-contango) — a fixed regime label, not a fitted split |
| Statistics | naive one-sample *t* and **Newey-West (HAC)** *t* at 3 lags on the daily gap (paired single series — no "other group" exists here, so Welch is used only for the stress-vs-rest regime split); Wilson interval on the hit rate; a **circular block-bootstrap** (block=21 sessions, 5,000 draws) CI/placebo for the mean gap |
| Execution / costs | one documented convention (third axis only): a constant-notional long-CL=F / short-USO book, **rebalanced monthly**; borrow named at 0.75%/yr on the short leg (a conservative easy-to-borrow-ETF assumption, not a crisis spike), costs = 2 × one-way × NAV charged only on rebalance days |
| Data quirks (named) | the May-2020 WTI front-month contract settled at **-$37.63** on 2020-04-20 — the only non-positive print on either tape. Log returns are undefined across it, so that day and its neighbor (2020-04-21) drop out of the continuous gap series automatically (`np.log` → NaN → `dropna`, no manual row surgery) and are instead treated as their own case study. USO executed a 1-for-8 reverse split on 2020-04-29 (folded in by `auto_adjust=True`) |

No survivorship: both USO and CL=F are the single live instrument/continuous-futures print
throughout — there is no basket to condition on survivors.

## The headline — cumulative divergence since USO's 2006-04-10 inception

| quantity | USO | CL=F |
|---|--:|--:|
| total return, 20.22 years | **-80.5%** | +0.8% |
| CAGR | **-7.76%/yr** | +0.04%/yr |
| CAGR gap (USO − CL=F) | **-7.80 pp/yr** | |

Twenty years of the same underlying commodity, two wildly different outcomes: the "oil price"
everyone quotes on a ticker is essentially flat over two decades, while the fund built to give
retail exposure to it lost **four-fifths of its value**.

## Daily roll-drag — the gap (USO − CL=F) per day

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| n (trading days) | 5,080 (2006-04-11 → 2026-06-30) |
| mean gap | **-0.0362%/day** (**-9.13%/yr**) |
| naive one-sample *t* | **-2.11** |
| Newey-West *t*, 5 / 21 / 63 lags | **-2.33** / -1.91 / -1.67 |
| hit rate (USO underperforms CL=F that day) | 2,579/5,080 = **50.8%** (Wilson 95% [49.4%, 52.1%]) |
| block-bootstrap (block=21, 5,000 draws) 95% CI, annualized | **[-20.2%, -1.7%]** |
| block-bootstrap p(mean ≥ 0) | **0.0038** |

The full-tape effect clears the desk bar at the standard daily-data lag (naive *t* = -2.11,
NW(5) *t* = -2.33) and the autocorrelation-robust block-bootstrap excludes zero outright
(*p* = 0.0038). **Caveat, said out loud:** longer HAC lags (21, 63 sessions — the roll-cycle
and quarterly horizons) fall just under the *t* = 2 bar. That is not noise-washing the
result — it is a *symptom* of what the regime split below shows directly: the drag is not a
smooth daily grind, it is **lumpy**, concentrated in a handful of crisis sessions whose extreme
kurtosis inflates any longer-lag variance estimate. And the down-day **hit rate is a coin flip
(50.8%)** — most days USO does *not* underperform CL=F; the divergence is a magnitude/skew
story (a few very bad days), not a frequency story.

## Contango-stress regimes — hardcoded 2009 / 2020 windows vs the rest of the tape

| regime | n | mean gap (ann.) | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| **stress windows (2009 + 2020)** | 229 (4.5% of days) | **-155.4%/yr** | **-2.06** |
| rest of the tape | 4,851 | -2.23%/yr | -0.80 |
| Welch *t* (stress vs rest) | | | **-2.03** |

| window | n | mean gap (ann.) | *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 2008-12-01 → 2009-06-30 (storage glut) | 146 | -61.1%/yr | -0.96 |
| 2020-03-01 → 2020-06-30 (COVID collapse) | 83 | -321.1%/yr | -1.84 |

**76.7% of the entire 20-year cumulative log-divergence** comes from those 229 days — 4.5% of
the sample. Outside the two named crisis windows, the daily gap is **not separately
certifiable** (*t* = -0.80) and averages only -2.2%/yr — a slow, largely noise-level bleed most
of the time, punctuated by two once-a-decade super-contango blowouts that do almost all of the
damage. This is the mechanism behind the caveat above: the process is not i.i.d., it is
regime-switching, and a single continuous-series HAC estimate at long lags is exactly what
gets diluted by that structure.

## Persistence check — does the drag survive dropping the worst episode?

*Added by an adversarial re-audit (2026-07): the regime split above already shows 76.7% of the
divergence concentrated in 4.5% of days, but "concentrated" is not the same claim as "not
persistent." This section tests persistence directly.*

| check | result |
|---|--:|
| naive *t*, excluding all of calendar-year 2020 (n=4,829) | **-1.15** (no longer separately certifiable) |
| NW(21) *t*, excluding all of 2020 | -1.92 |
| mean gap, excluding all of 2020 (ann.) | -3.86%/yr |
| block-bootstrap 95% CI, excluding all of 2020 | [-7.8%, -0.1%]/yr (narrowly excludes 0) |
| calendar years with negative gap | **13 / 21** (62%) |
| calendar years with positive gap | 8 / 21 — including **every year from 2021 through 2026** |
| post-2020 subsample (2021-01-04 → 2026-06-30, n=1,378, 5.48 yr) | USO **+228.7%** vs CL=F **+45.9%** |
| post-2020 mean gap (ann.) | **+14.84%/yr** (USO *ahead* of CL=F) |
| post-2020 naive *t* / NW(21) *t* | **+2.52** / **+4.47** |
| post-2020 block-bootstrap 95% CI | **[+8.7%, +21.8%]/yr** (entirely positive, excludes 0) |

Dropping 2020 alone knocks the naive *t* from -2.11 to -1.15 — below the standard bar. The
calendar-year sign count is a majority (13/21) but far from the "almost every year" persistence a
mechanical, structural tax would imply. Most decisively: the five-and-a-half years since the 2020
crisis rolled off (2021-01-04 → 2026-06-30) show USO **beating** CL=F by **+14.84%/yr**, a gap
that is itself statistically real by every measure used elsewhere in this study (naive *t* =
+2.52, NW(21) *t* = +4.47, block-bootstrap CI entirely above zero). This is the same roll
mechanism running in reverse: WTI spent most of 2021-2026 in **backwardation** (near month
pricier than far month, driven by post-COVID supply constraints and the 2022 supply shock), so
the monthly roll *collected* carry instead of paying it. **"USO mechanically loses to oil because
of contango" is not a standing law — contango and backwardation both happen, and the fund's gap
against CL=F tracks which one the market is in, not a fixed structural drag.** The 76.7%/4.5%
concentration finding still stands as a fact about *this* 20-year sample, but it describes two
large, real, non-repeating storage crises — not a mechanism that reliably fires most years.

## The April-2020 negative-oil episode (simple returns; log undefined across the sign flip)

| date | USO close | USO day return | CL=F close | CL=F day return |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2020-04-17 | 33.68 | -3.44% | 18.27 | -8.05% |
| **2020-04-20** | 30.00 | **-10.93%** | **-37.63** | **-305.97%** |
| 2020-04-21 | 22.48 | -25.07% | 10.01 | -126.60% (arithmetic, across a sign flip) |
| 2020-04-22 | 20.08 | -10.68% | 13.78 | +37.66% |
| 2020-04-23 | 21.12 | +5.18% | 16.50 | +19.74% |

On the single most extreme day in oil-market history — the front WTI contract settling
**negative** — USO fell a painful but perfectly ordinary-looking **-10.9%**, not -306%. By
April 2020 USO already held a laddered basket across contract months (a structure the fund
pushed further that same month, alongside its 2020-04-29 1-for-8 reverse split), so it never
"owned" the collapsing May contract at anything like full weight. USO still lost **-40.4%**
cumulatively over the following week (2020-04-17 close → 2020-04-22 close) — it did not escape
the episode — but the headline "USO went negative too" folklore is simply false, and the
"USO = oil" mental model breaks in **both directions** on the one day that mattered most.

## Third axis — the "long spot / short USO" carry-capture book

Constant-notional long CL=F / short USO, rebalanced to notional on the first trading day of
each month; 0.75%/yr borrow on the short leg (named, conservative), 2 × one-way cost × NAV
charged only on rebalance days.

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| gross | **+9.13%/yr**, vol 19.4%, Sharpe **0.47**, max drawdown -58.8%, worst day -14.2% |
| net @ 5 bps | **+7.17%/yr**, Sharpe 0.37, max drawdown -62.9% |
| net @ 10 bps | +5.97%/yr, Sharpe 0.31, max drawdown -65.2% |
| HAC(21) *t* on the daily book return | **+1.91** |
| sign-shuffle placebo | *p* = **0.0130** |
| net@5bps, **excluding** the 2009/2020 stress windows | **+0.27%/yr**, Sharpe **0.02** (n = 4,851) |
| net@5bps, **inside** the stress windows only | +153.4%/yr (illustrative; n = 229 days), Sharpe 2.13 |

The book looks tradable at a glance (net Sharpe 0.37, positive at both cost levels) — until you
ask *when* it made its money. **Strip out the 229 stress-window days and the net return is
+0.27%/yr at Sharpe 0.02 — indistinguishable from zero.** Essentially the entire multi-decade
P&L of "long spot, short USO" comes from correctly holding the trade through exactly the 2009
and 2020 storage crises — two events that, by their nature, cannot be forecast, and there is no
guarantee a third ever recurs on the same schedule. For 95.5% of calendar time the position pays
you almost nothing after a modest, realistic borrow fee, while still carrying a -63% peak
drawdown in the full backtest and needing continuous access to USO short inventory (thinnest
exactly when a storage crisis makes everyone want to short it).

## Synthetic positive control — the machinery is unbiased

Deterministic (spot, fund) return pair: a plain random walk "spot" and a "fund" equal to spot
minus a TUNABLE daily drag plus extra drag on two synthetic stress blocks, plus small
independent tracking noise (so a zero-drag null still has a well-defined, non-degenerate gap);
no network.

| world | naive *t* | NW(5) *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| null (drag = 0), **20 seeds** | mean **-0.09** (sd 0.80), **\|t\| ≥ 2 in 0/20 seeds** | |
| planted drag (3 bps/day + 300 bps in the 2 synthetic stress blocks) | **-16.31** | **-7.64** |

The detector never fires on the null and lights up sharply on a planted drag. *(A
faithful-engine / power check only — never cited in support of the real-tape stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** USO lost **80.5%** while CL=F was **+0.8%** over the same 20.22 years
  (CAGR gap **-7.80 pp/yr**), and the full-sample daily gap looks decisive at first pass (naive
  *t* = -2.11, NW(5) *t* = -2.33, block-bootstrap excludes zero at *p* = 0.0038). But the
  persistence check above overturns the "mechanical, structural" reading: **76.7%** of the
  divergence comes from just **4.5%** of days (the 2009/2020 crisis windows); excluding all of
  2020 drops the naive *t* to **-1.15** (no longer separately certifiable); only **13/21**
  calendar years are negative; and the **post-2020 subsample (2021-2026, 5.48 years)** reverses
  sign entirely — USO **beat** CL=F by **+14.84%/yr**, itself statistically real (naive *t* =
  +2.52, NW(21) *t* = +4.47, bootstrap CI entirely positive). The roll mechanism is genuine but
  bidirectional (contango vs. backwardation); it is not the persistent, one-way structural tax
  the "USO mechanically loses to oil" folklore claims — it is two large, real, non-repeating
  crisis episodes.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The long-CL=F/short-USO book *looks* tradable in full-sample
  backtest (net Sharpe 0.37 at 5 bps) but its HAC(21) *t* (+1.91) misses the bar, stripping
  the two named crisis windows leaves **+0.27%/yr at Sharpe 0.02**, and the book would have run
  net *negative* through the entire 2021-2026 backwardation stretch — the entire realized edge
  is two historical storage crises you could not have timed in advance, against a -63% max
  drawdown and thin short-borrow exactly when the trade would matter most.
- **"Does USO let you own oil the way retail investors think?" — BUSTED.** Down 80% against a
  flat headline oil price over the first 15 years, then **+14.8%/yr ahead of it** over the last
  5.5, and on the day oil made history (front WTI settling at **-$37.63**) USO barely flinched
  (-10.9%, not -306%). It was never holding "the oil price" in the first place — the ETF is not
  a spot-crude proxy in any direction, in any regime.
